facts.fact: Carol Roberts' NADA article sorts discus into 14 classes: Classes 1–4 are wild discus and Classes 5–14 are domestic, tank-bred strains.
Wild classes: Class 1 Heckel, Class 2 Brown (S. aequifasciata axelrodi), Class 3 Blue (S. a. haraldi), Class 4 Green (S. a. aequifasciata).
Pattern classes: Class 5 Thick Line, Class 6 Thin Line, Class 7 Pattern, Class 8 Spotted, Class 9 Open Pattern.
Colour classes: Class 10 Blue, Class 11 Red, Class 12 Yellow, Class 13 White, Class 14 Open.
Discus classes are not fixed: at a show, the owner picks the class each fish is entered in.
All discus can interbreed and produce fertile fry.
In Heckel discus, three of the nine vertical bars stand out more than the rest: the bar through the eye, the fifth (middle) bar and the tail bar.
Heckel discus have nine vertical bars, and the middle one is clearly thicker.
Wild Red Spotted Greens have a greenish-tan base colour, and collectors prefer fish with spots over a large part of the body.
Thick Line (Class 5) fish have vertical stress bars with thick, straight striations; Turquoise is the example given.
Thin Line (Class 6) fish have fine striations. Snakeskins belong here; most have 14 vertical bars plus fine lines and dots on the gill plates.
Snakeskin discus have 12 to 18 vertical bars instead of nine.
The Pattern class (Class 7) covers complicated striations, such as Ring Leopard, as well as Checkerboard and Pearl.
The Spotted class (Class 8) includes Red Leopards, domestic Red Spotted Greens and leopard-spotted Snakeskins.
Open Pattern (Class 9) takes any pattern, for example Albino Spotted, Albino Snakeskin or Golden Leopard Snakeskin.

Example fish in the colour classes: Blue includes Blue Diamond and Cobalt; Red is any red discus; Yellow includes Pigeon Blood, Golden, Yellow Crystal and Golden Spotted; White includes Snow White and white Pigeon Blood; Open includes Yellow White, Red White, Calico and Ghost.
Vertical stress bars occur in wild discus and most domestic strains, but Pigeon Blood, Blue Diamond and White discus lack them. In a spawn, the bars are the first trait you can see.
Striations are horizontal markings laid over the base colour and are classed as either thick line or thin line.
'Pattern' means the markings over the base colour, such as spots, striations or pearl.
Blue Diamonds count as 'solid blue', with no striations on the face or fins; Snow Whites count as 'solid white'.
Pepper is small black specks on the nose and face that pigeon-based discus share; it shows more when the fish is stressed or ill.
Early Pigeon Bloods were heavily covered in black pepper, but there is much less of it in Pigeon Bloods sold today.
Eye colour by strain: Snakeskins have red or amber eyes; Ghosts and Whites have mostly white eyes with black pupils; Albinos have pink eyes; Blue Diamonds and Pigeon Bloods have amber or red eyes.
Pigeon Blood has no vertical stress bars, and its colour ranges from white or yellow through orange to nearly red.
Pigeon Blood is dominant: a pure Pigeon Blood crossed with any other discus gives all Pigeon Blood fry.
Blue Diamond is recessive: two Blue Diamonds give all Blue Diamond fry.
Heckel discus was described by Heckel in 1840 and comes from the Rio Negro (Manaus) area. Green discus was described by Pellegrin in 1904. Schultz described the Brown and Blue subspecies in 1960.
Some taxonomists hold that there is only one species and that the subspecies are just regional colour forms.

American breeders produced Turquoise and Cobalt in the 1970s, and Red Turquoise came out of Europe in the same period. Ghost, Blue Diamond, Snakeskin and Pigeon Blood were developed in Asia in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Snow White appeared in the late 1990s.
Pigeon Blood was developed in Thailand, and Ghost came from a Brilliant Blue mutation.
A proposed show standard would judge pattern fish on base colour and surface (overlay) colour, shine, the contrast between surface and base colour, and how evenly the pattern is spread.
The same proposal judges solid fish on how even the body colour is, with separate grades for 100% solid and 90% solid fish.
The proposed standard would give no extra points for fish above the optimal size, to discourage growing fish artificially large.

Vietnamese names for the 14 classes: dĩa heckel, dĩa nâu, dĩa lam and dĩa lục (wild Heckel, Brown, Blue, Green); chỉ dày (Thick Line); chỉ mỏng (Thin Line); hoa văn (Pattern); đốm (Spotted); hoa văn tự do (Open Pattern); lam, đỏ, vàng and trắng (Solid Blue, Red, Yellow, White); màu tự do (Open).

Vietnamese colour terms: màu gốc (primary colour) is the colour of the young fish; màu áo (secondary colour) is the colour of the adult; màu nền (base colour) is the colour between the lines, usually brown, red, orange or yellow, and in places such as the head it can be the primary colour itself; đơn sắc = solid colour. The forum's plate shows four primary colours: brown, beige, grey and cream.
Vietnamese keepers call the vertical stress bars 'can'. They show strongly when the fish is frightened, and how many there are depends on the strain.

'Vùng D' (D area) is the middle of the body behind the head, inside a D-shaped outline (drawn on the forum's diagram). In a solid fish it is one colour (lines are allowed on the head, gill covers and fin tips); in a pattern fish it carries lines and spots in several metallic tones over the base colour. A fish whose pattern does not fill the D area goes in Open Pattern (Class 9).

Vietnamese strain names: bông đỏ = Red Turquoise, bông xanh = Blue Turquoise, hạt lựu = Checkerboard, bồ câu = Pigeon Blood, da rắn = Snakeskin, beo = Leopard, khoen = Ring, bạch ngọc = Snow White, bạch điệp = White Butterfly, lam Đức or lam A = Cobalt, lam phấn = Blue Diamond, bạch tạng = Albino. In the blue class, 'lam A' is the blue fish and 'lục B' the green one (Ocean Green).

Vietnamese terms used in describing discus: viền (rim) = the band of metallic colour along the dorsal and anal fins; chỉ (line, stripe) = the metallic lines on head, body and fins, and lines and spots together make the pattern; con ngươi = pupil; tròng mắt = eye ring. Most discus have a naturally red eye ring, while albinos have a pink or maroon pupil, so calling an albino 'red-eyed' is ambiguous.
A Vietnamese discus farm sells Blue Diamond as 'cá dĩa lam phấn'.
Some Vietnamese shops sell Blue Diamond as 'cá dĩa lam Đức', the name the forum gives to Cobalt.
